articles.title: What are the Aukus submarines actually for? It’s a question the government refuses to answer
articles.summary: Australia should end the Aukus submarine plan and pursue a properly tested strategy to replace the Collins class fleet
body: In 1998 I was appointed chief of the Australian defence force. I spent much of my career handling classified information and I understand why some things must stay secret: operational plans, intelligence sources, the capabilities on which lives depend.
But there is a difference between protecting secrets and withholding reasons. On Aukus, Australians have been denied the reasons.

That is the significant lesson I take from serving as a commissioner on the Aukus public inquiry. The government and the opposition declined written invitations to give evidence. No one serving in the Australian Defence Organisation appeared. This means the case for the most expensive defence project in our history – likely to be more than $368bn by the mid-2050s – was never put to us.
Related: We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?

Instead, we heard from other Australians – young people, their mums and dads, and First Nations Australians – who cannot get straight answers about Aukus and its implications for them. They want to know about the nuclear issues – the waste from the submarine program and the rotation of American and British nuclear-powered submarines through Western Australia, and they want to know about the costs and why Australia is actively supporting submarine building in the US and UK through unconditional financial support.

The government may say it has not been silent. The Australian Submarine Agency has produced fact sheets, a public report and corporate plans. They assert that “only nuclear-powered submarines, acquired through the Aukus partnership, will meet Australia’s defence requirements in the decades ahead”, and that conventional submarines will be “increasingly less able to meet Australia’s needs”. They promise a “strategy of denial” and “impactful projection”. But they do not show the working: which missions, compared with what alternatives, at what cost and with what risk. An assertion is not an explanation.
Let’s start with the simplest question: what are these submarines for?

Nuclear-powered submarines are formidable machines. Their distinctive advantage is speed and endurance underwater, sustainable over long distances, but they are not much good in shallow water. Their characteristics matter most for two missions: hunting other nuclear-powered submarines, including those capable of launching nuclear weapons, and keeping pace underwater with American aircraft carrier battle groups. Conventional submarines can perform most of the other tasks Australia needs.

Impactful projection where, and against whom? If the real purpose is to hunt Chinese submarines near China’s home ports, or to escort American carriers, the government should say so – and explain why these missions serve Australia.

Alone it would be madness for us to take on China. The only plausible way we would be fighting near China’s coast is in a war begun by the United States. Building our future defence force around that possibility is a profound choice, and Australians deserve to have it put to them honestly.

Instead, it looks like this acquisition has become the strategy. We have a recent national defence strategy but there is no national security strategy to show what we are protecting, from what, and how diplomacy, the economy, climate resilience and defence fit together. The United States and the United Kingdom, our partners in Aukus, have published theirs. We should publish ours.
Meanwhile, commitments are being locked in.

From 2027, HMAS Stirling, the navy base near Perth, will host a rotating force of up to four American nuclear-powered submarines and one British. These will not be occasional visits as has been the practice till now. The government has committed up to $8bn to expand the base. Housing is being arranged for American personnel and their families – in a region where people told our inquiry about homelessness on their own doorstep.
Related: Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?

Australia has agreed by treaty to take responsibility for disposing of the spent fuel – highly enriched uranium – from its own submarines. The submarine agency’s own corporate plan names its failure to build disposal capability as a key risk, yet it sets no target, timeline or measure for dealing with the waste. Nuclear waste disposal will not be a new conversation for our community but it will be weapons-grade waste – and that is new!

The government says the foreign submarines will be conventionally armed for now – but what about into the future? The US is developing a nuclear-armed cruise missile for its Virginia-class boats. In supporting the Treaty of Rarotonga what conditions will Australia set, and how will they be verified? Could Stirling support nuclear strike operations even if no weapon is stored ashore? Will Stirling become a target for nuclear strike? If so, how will it be protected?
Money already committed is not a reason to commit more. Nor is urgency an excuse to skip strategy.

We have been here before. As a young naval officer, I worked with my bosses on the program to replace the aircraft carrier HMAS Melbourne. The program had been keenly debated for years under the Fraser governments before the Hawke government was elected in 1983. Within two weeks of taking office, it scrapped the carrier program. It then reviewed Australia’s strategic position through a new lens and built a new defence force around contemporary and prospective strategic needs. The Dibb review of 1986 and the 1987 defence white paper are examples of the kind of work we need to do now. It is urgent.

Our report recommends ending the Aukus submarine plan. That is not an argument against submarines. Australia needs a credible submarine capability under full Australian command and control, and a properly tested plan to replace the Collins class – a submarine chosen to suit our missions, not missions chosen to suit the submarine.

Above all, we must safeguard our capacity to decide for ourselves. Sovereignty is not ownership of a submarine or flying a flag over a base. It is the ability of an Australian government to decide what to do in Australia’s interests, including when our allies would prefer otherwise. The test is not whether we can say yes – that may look easy, but it will be hard. It is whether we can say no – and that is likely to be the toughest decision an Australia government has to make.
• Admiral Chris Barrie AC RAN R’td was chief of the Australian defence force from 1998 to 2002 and is a commissioner on the Aukus public inquiry

articles.title: The night-sky image so incredible the NZ man behind it has been accused of using AI
articles.summary: Brendan Larsen spent hours taking hundreds of photographs of the sky over a mountain in New Zealand
body: A photograph showing thousands of satellites cross-hatching the night sky over New Zealand appeared so extraordinary the astrophotographer who captured it is fighting accusations it was created by AI.

To create his spectacular image – now viewed millions of times online – Brendan Larsen spent two hours in September snapping hundreds of photographs of the night sky over Mount Taranaki in the North Island.

Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”

The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 40 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites.
“I could start to see the pattern emerging and realised: ‘Wow, this looks really awesome.’ I knew if I carried on it would look even better and more impressive in terms of satellite numbers.”
The resulting image shows the sky inundated with about 1,400 satellites and 14,000 trails forming a dense crisscrossing pattern above the mountain.

When Larsen uploaded the image to his social media channels in mid-October, it quickly went viral, gaining him 15,000 new followers, clocking up tens of millions of views and igniting thousands of comments.

Some viewers dismissed the photo as AI – but Larsen understands why. “AI generating software is becoming so good it is becoming difficult to tell AI images from real images … especially if you’re not familiar with the location or with astrophotography,” he says. Still, it is “frustrating”.
It is also exasperating, he says, to see his image downloaded and recreated by AI, with obvious flaws.
In anticipation of the AI accusations and backlash, Larsen documented his creative process on video, which he hopes will also allow viewers to form an emotional connection to the landscape.

As a child Larsen was “absolutely blown away” by the number of stars over parts of rural New Zealand. But he has noticed an increase in light pollution and the number of satellites over the six years he has been photographing the sky.
Related: Total solar eclipse books out hotels two years in advance in New Zealand city
“It’s interesting and fascinating seeing satellites, but it’s also disturbing,” he says.

“I’ve got about 10,000 comments on my Facebook page … nine out of 10 of the comments are like: ‘Wow, beautiful photo, but horrifying, terrifying and really concerning about what’s happening to the night sky.’”
About 16,000 working satellites are circling the planet, alongside tens of thousands of defunct spacecrafts, rocket parts and debris from payloads breaking up.

Studies have warned that metal particles from space activities – such as rocket launches and satellite reentries – could affect atmospheric chemistry and the ozone layer, while the UN has warned increased space activity poses risks to ground safety, darkness and astronomy.

While satellites don’t yet overwhelm the sky to the naked eye, Larsen worries about the future state of the night sky. He hopes his image will ignite debate and reflection over how satellites can be used responsibly.
“We can raise awareness, and through that get a groundswell of support for protecting the night sky.”

articles.title: King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow
articles.summary: Speaking in Antigua, the king did not give explicit support for reparations but said he wanted to ‘address past wrongs’
body: King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.
“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past.

“The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”
Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs.

But the king stopped short of an apology or explicit support for reparations, instead pointing to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage.
“For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.

Though speaking as head of the Commonwealth, and this speech would have been drafted by Charles personally along with his advisers, palace aides have indicated there would be “no surprises” in it for the UK government.
Andy Burnham refused to be drawn on whether the UK might offer further financial contributions to the Commonwealth stopping short of direct reparations.
The UK prime minister told reporters: “I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations, and I made that quite abundantly clear in the piece that I wrote in advance of coming here.

“But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got, green finance. That’s what we’ve done under all governments, and in my view, we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth.”

Pressed on whether this could mean additional financial contributions that would weigh on the taxpayer, Burnham said: “Well, you’re getting ahead. What we need to have is that meaningful dialogue where we take time to listen, and let’s be clear: the Commonwealth is an important part of our trade too.

“It’s a two-way arrangement. You know, trade is up between the UK and the rest of the Commonwealth in the last year quite significantly, actually. So you need to see it in that way as well. It benefits Britain to be here, listening to people, building that new partnership, and that’s good for growth in Britain.”

Reparations are not formally on the agenda of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), where trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and opportunities for young people were among the stated priorities of the 56-member bloc.
But sustained campaigning by Caribbean governments and a growing international reparations movement have propelled the issue to the centre of political debate surrounding the gathering.

Opening the summit in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, the country’s prime minister, Gaston Browne, said “fairness” required an “honest engagement with our shared history” and called for meaningful and respectful dialogue on reparatory justice and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism.
Burnham had said he was open to Britain apologising for slavery, with officials holding talks with national leaders in Antigua about what that could entail.
He has also proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

But Caribbean leaders have stressed that dialogue must extend beyond an apology. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), described an apology as an “essential first step” but said an “apology without repair is incomplete”.

He said any structured dialogue must allow consideration of the entirety of Caricom’s 10-point reparations plan, including public health, education, cultural restitution, psychological rehabilitation, debt cancellation and monetary compensation.

Britain’s royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology. A palace spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the king to announce a change in government policy.

According to the AFP news agency, Burnham discussed slavery with the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral meetings the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.
They discussed how Britain was “offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade”, including the “next steps”, Downing Street said.
Outside the heavily secured summit venue, protesters gathered with placards declaring: “We know what you did and we can see you,” and “You say appalling atrocity, yet you refuse to apologise.”

One protester, Lenworth Johnson, said that if the king’s constitutional position prevented him from apologising, the British government should authorise him to do so. “We feel an apology is necessary,” he said.
Related: UK makes huge aid cuts to Commonwealth nations despite warm words at Chogm

Another, Radcliffe Robins, said the wealth enjoyed by Britain and other western powers was built in part on enslavement. “It is absolutely necessary that his majesty the king and the royal family apologise for the brutality and the injustice that they have imposed on us,” he said. “And with that, we ask for reparations.”
Another protester said the demonstration was intended to ensure those entering the summit knew campaigners were “watching them and listening to what they’re saying and what they’re doing”.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda Reparations Support Commission and one of the organisers, said: “One whose heart is filled with horror and whose soul bears the most profound personal sorrow must surely be moved beyond words – beyond repeated emotional expression without acceptance of responsibility.

“Genuine moral consciousness demands apologies – the acknowledgment of wrong, the acceptance of responsibility and the commitment to pursue reparations. Unfortunately King Charles III does nothing of the sort. He has again failed the people who recognise him as king.”
The demonstrations followed a reparations event on Monday hosted by the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations alongside campaign organisations.
Its chair, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, welcomed debt relief but warned against presenting it as reparations.

“Reparations was never about personal guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions that still stand,” she said. “Aid is not reparations, because aid leaves the power with the giver. Agency was the crime. Agency has to be the remedy.”

The meeting was followed by a candlelight vigil on an Antiguan beach commemorating enslaved Africans brought to the island. The Rev Bonnie Smith, president of the Antigua Christian Council, asked those gathered to remember people torn from their homes, separated from their families and forced across the Atlantic into enslavement.
Related: Memo to King Charles: if the Dutch king can apologise for slavery, why can’t you? | Raoul de Jong
“Their names may be absent from our records, but they are not absent from your love,” she said. “Their voices may have been silenced, but their lives have never ceased to matter.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, meanwhile framed the campaign as part of a wider struggle for peace and justice.
“We are concerned about the unleashing of terror and violence upon innocent people,” he said.
“We believe that reparatory justice that calls for human decency, equality and justice for all is the philosophy that will hold us together as humanity going into this 21st century.”

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair Campaign, the reparatory justice movement, said he believed Charles’s expressions of sorrow over slavery were sincere, but was disappointed he had not gone any further than his previous remarks.
“The apology hasn’t come. And there’s no talk about reparatory justice. So to that extent, this speech to me was a disappointment,” he said.
The king’s reference to support for health, education and infrastructure, Gonsalves said, concerned subjects already covered in the agreements in the UN sustainable development goals.
“What we are saying is that there has to be, additionally … a special carve-out in respect of reparatory justice,” he added.

articles.title: One dead and another missing in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.summary: The incident took place in the same province where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren last November
body: A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.

On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online.

Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.

Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast. Its remote location and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.

Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.

“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” said Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.”
Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.

articles.title: Britain must have the courage to face its legacy of slavery
articles.summary: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Andy Burnham in which he says that people today can’t be held personally liable for the country’s historical wrongs
body: In his opinion piece (30 October), Andy Burnham argues that British people today cannot be held liable for historical wrongs “in which they played no personal part”. On one level, he is right. But he confuses two very different things: personal liability and the continuing responsibility of the state.

When slavery was abolished in the British empire in 1833, the government borrowed £20m – an extraordinary sum then – to compensate enslavers for the loss of their supposed property. Some 40,000 claims were made. The British taxpayer carried the cost, and the resulting public debt was not finally cleared until 2015.

Around 3,000 people in Britain received about half of the compensation fund. The state had effectively used public money to preserve the wealth of a privileged elite, while leaving the victims of slavery uncompensated.

If the state could identify enslavers and establish their claims to compensation in 1833, it cannot be beyond the capacity of today’s state to examine how that wealth, and its enduring legacy, might be addressed. The historical records are remarkably detailed, after all.
The state cannot claim continuity when honouring its obligations to enslavers while disowning any responsibility towards the enslaved. It is the same institution, enduring across generations.

Nobody is suggesting that today’s citizens should inherit personal guilt for the actions of their ancestors. But neither should the wealth accumulated through slavery be treated as a private inheritance, cleansed of its origins simply by the passage of time.

The descendants of enslavers, many of whose families remain among Britain’s wealthiest, cannot just divorce their inherited privilege from the injustice that helped create it. They too have a responsibility to confront that legacy.Giselle DyeEdinburgh

• Andy Burnham celebrates British resistance to slavery while refusing to recognise the totality of the system against which people resisted. Recovering these histories matters, including that of enslaved people’s struggles. But we also need to understand how chattel enslavement and imperialism developed a global political economy organised through racial hierarchy, capitalist exploitation and patriarchal power.

These processes shaped who could own property, whose labour could be appropriated, and whose lives mattered. Their consequences persist in the distribution of wealth and power today. This system harmed people differently. Enslaved Africans and colonised peoples endured dispossession and violence on a scale incomparable with workers’ exploitation in Britain, but their struggles were interconnected.
Patriarchy sustained this order by exploiting women’s labour and controlling reproduction. Ecological destruction accompanied the treatment of land and life as resources for extraction.

Imperial competition drove these processes; wealth extracted through empire enriched Britain, disproportionately benefiting its landed elites. And yet Burnham writes of climate change, women’s rights and the cost of living crisis as if these issues are disconnected – as though each can be resolved independently within the very system that generated the harm.

Reparatory justice doesn’t depend on individuals having personally committed violence; it begins with these relationships. Most of us never had the opportunity to learn how they shaped past harms and continue to harm others and ourselves. An adequate response requires material redistribution and debt cancellation, alongside public education and discussion.

A parliamentary inquiry that tells the truth of the British empire is critical: how it developed, who was harmed and who benefited, how its structures persist and what repair now requires. Past solidarity should encourage us to confront these connections; celebrating earlier generations’ courage while refusing to see the wood for the trees leaves the structures they challenged far too comfortably intact.Dr Asha Herten-CrabbUniversity of Warwick

• Andy Burnham is open to an apology for Britain’s role in slavery, but rejects financial reparations. He argues that historical wrongs “happened in a different age under different laws” and that British people today played no personal part in them.

For centuries, Britain was a leading slave-trading nation. Burnham instead emphasises its leading role in the abolition movement, which began in the 18th century. The question, however, is whether the absence of personal involvement removes responsibility for injustices whose consequences persist.

Past injustices matter today if they have left morally relevant traces in the present, meaning that there are people today who suffer from the past injustices and people who gain. There is, for example, a direct link between slavery and the slave trade on the one hand, and the current poverty and underdevelopment in the Caribbean on the other. There is also a link between the incomes from slavery and the slave trade that rolled into the British economy in the 17th to 19th centuries and present prosperity.

In principle, if someone gains and someone else suffers from a historical wrong, and the heir of the perpetrator is aware of this relation, there is a moral duty for the one who gains to compensate the one who suffers. Therefore Britain has a moral duty to compensate the Caribbean nations that suffer from past injustices. An apology is not enough, but compensation can of course take various forms.Göran CollsteEmeritus professor of applied ethics, Linköping University; author, Global Rectificatory Justice

• Andy Burnham’s openness to offering an apology for British involvement in slavery is a welcome development. But despite his recognition of its “brutal and barbaric violation” of the enslaved, he still manages to make an “honest conversation about the legacies of slavery” seem like an act of political largesse rather than an objective audit of structural inequality.

If he really understood how transatlantic slavery “still shapes our world today” he might reflect on some of its local ironies. For example, the fact that, though not “liable for historical wrongs”, British people nonetheless, through taxation, serviced the debt that compensated enslavers (some of the wealthiest people in the country) until as recently as 2015. He would recognise the insult added to that injury for some of those taxpayers, who were descendants of the enslaved.

In fact, if Burnham truly understood historical legacies in the Caribbean and elsewhere, he might consider cancelling Commonwealth debt repayments altogether, rather than proposing to lengthen the term over which they are repaid. He might recognise that the “cup of sorrow” referenced in his quote from the abolitionist Thomas Clarkson did not disappear in 1807 at the end of the slave trade or in 1833 with emancipation, and would comprehend the extent to which slavery shaped colonial attitudes and practices, replacing a barbaric yoke with an authoritarian one.

He would see that the effects of slavery are not something to be recognised only in an annual ritual of remorse during Black History Month; neither are they redeemed by politically empty declarations to “end global poverty and inequality”, while denying the legitimacy of some of the reparative means to even attempt it.Paul McGilchristCromer, Norfolk

articles.title: UK makes huge aid cuts to Commonwealth nations despite warm words at Chogm
articles.summary: Nations in the group fare worse than others, with funding for nature projects especially hard hit even as climate crisis intensifies global need
body: The UK government has slashed overseas aid to Commonwealth countries, the Guardian can reveal, in contrast to the warm words for the group from King Charles and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, this week.
Amid sharp cuts in the UK’s aid budget overall, the Commonwealth has fared poorly, an analysis of the most recent and projected aid figures, seen by the Guardian, has shown.

Funding from the UK to the Commonwealth nations that previously had bilateral aid programmes will be cut from £546m in 2024-25 to £131m in 2028-29. Of that total, a large chunk – £68m – will go to Nigeria, leaving £63m for other countries.

The revelations come as the king attends the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) this week in Antigua, where he said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices” of slavery but where Burnham’s government fought to ensure that any discussion of reparations would be off the agenda.

The government has been cutting back on aid to countries that have been rapidly developing and are now judged to be middle income, such as India and Antigua, but the cuts to Commonwealth countries go much further, including many countries that are still among the poorest and many that are struggling under heavy debt burdens.

For example, Sierra Leone, one of the world’s least developed countries, will have its aid slashed from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. The UK and Sierra Leone will act as co-conveners of a strand of talks focusing on adaptation to the impacts of the climate crisis, at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey next week.

Aid to Rwanda, where the previous government had a scheme to send refugees, is also being cut from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. Aid to Tanzania will be slashed from £60m in 2025-26 to £5m in 2028-29. The Caribbean Development Team will have its funding cut from more than £98m in 2025-26 to £45m in 2026-27.
Nigeria will continue to represent one of the biggest destinations for Commonwealth aid, scheduled to receive £68m in 2028-29, down from £137m this year.

Funding for nature has been particularly hard-hit, experts told the Guardian, as many Commonwealth countries have not only had their aid funding slashed but have also been cut off from applying to the Darwin Initiative funds for nature protection. At least 26 countries from the Commonwealth have been prevented from receiving funds under the longstanding Darwin funding stream, worth about £40m a year.

Adrian Gahan, the UK lead at the Campaign for Nature charity, said: “UK aid to Commonwealth countries has fallen dramatically in recent years, with further cuts on the horizon. Some of the world’s most biodiversity-rich countries, many of which are also grappling with high levels of poverty, are facing severe reductions in support. For example, the UK’s Caribbean Development Team is set to see its funding cut by more than half between this year and next.”

He noted the contrast between the government’s stance at Chogm and the royal visit to the Caribbean. “This week, the king attended the launch of the Commonwealth nature initiative, a major new effort to protect nature across Commonwealth countries,” said Gahan. “Yet the UK government failed to make a financial contribution.”

Jean McLean, Oxfam GB chief influencing officer, said: “The UK government has really dropped the ball when it comes to the aid budget at exactly the moment when conflict, humanitarian crises, hunger and climate breakdown are driving global need to record levels. These cuts will not be felt in Westminster – they will be felt by families facing starvation, children denied healthcare and education, and communities struggling to survive the impacts of conflict and climate disasters.”
The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has been approached for comment. The Chogm meeting is set to wrap up on Wednesday.

articles.title: Seven planes across Europe searched or diverted after ‘malicious hoax’ bomb threats
articles.summary: Unclear if series of incidents affecting two UK departures and several Ryanair services, among others, were connected
body: Seven planes across Europe have been searched or diverted after a series of bomb threats were made to passenger flights, prompting questions as to whether there was any coordination behind the warnings.

Two UK departures – one from Heathrow and one from Manchester – were among those threatened in what Downing Street called “malicious hoaxes”, though all planes landed safely and no explosives were found.

A UK Department for Transport source added that the low-level threats were “not credible” and that passengers should not be concerned, though the warnings disrupted flights and prompted investigations across the UK and Europe.
None of the incidents and subsequent searches threw up any evidence of terrorist activity, though authorities were responding to an unusual number of reported threats in one day.

One of Warsaw’s two main airports, Modlin, was briefly closed after receiving a diverted plane, and Polish officials confirmed that they had received bomb threats involving two flights coming into the capital.

Italian fighter jets escorted a Ryanair plane into Rome following a warning of a suspected threat on a flight coming from Dublin. The flight landed safely and nothing untoward was reported as being found.

There was little obvious pattern surrounding the incidents, which affected flights taking off from the UK, Ireland, Denmark, Portugal and Italy, and landing in Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria. Four of the flights were operated by Ryanair, the others by Wizz Air, LOT and SAS.

Investigators added there was no immediate evidence of a hostile state being behind the threats, though they continued to monitor developments, sharing information across the continent while inquiries continued.

Aviation security fears have been reignited with the recent FlyDubai incident when a co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane. Russia has also been accused of being behind firebomb threats targeting parcel carriers using cargo planes over the past two years.
The threats followed an incident on Monday when another flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted, apparently without substance.

Experts said that fake threats occur on a daily basis. Philip Baum, visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, said: “Most are from individuals who think it is funny or want to delay a flight for some reason. If the industry was to respond to every unsubstantiated threat, flights would grind to a halt.
“The reality is that terrorist organisations who might like to smuggle a bomb on to a flight don’t tell people, they claim responsibility after the attacks.”
But he added that the fact that some aircraft did divert would “imply that the threats are credible and specific in nature, and therefore one has to respond accordingly”.

Tuesday’s series of incidents started with a flight from Heathrow operated by the Polish carrier LOT, which was scheduled to arrive at Warsaw’s Chopin airport but was diverted to the second airport, further from the Polish capital, Modlin. Authorities closed that airport after the alert and the Boeing 737 Max landed without incident.
“The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found,” spokesperson Adam Szablowski told AFP. “The airport has been reopened and is operating normally.”

A Scandinavian Airlines plane from Copenhagen to Warsaw was also the subject of a threat but landed at Chopin airport, where a security inspection that did not turn up any explosive devices closed part of the airport.

Another UK departure, a Ryanair plane from Manchester, was met by emergency vehicles on landing at its destination, Murcia in southern Spain, after another threat. Spanish regional authorities confirmed on social media that no explosives were found on the flight.
The Metropolitan police confirmed its aviation unit is monitoring the situation, adding no security issues were identified following threats made against flights after they had taken off.

A UK government spokesperson said of the threats to two departures from Britain: “The UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we’ve seen today.
“Our world-leading police and intelligence agencies work closely every day to keep us safe, using the tools they have to assess and respond to potential threats.”

In Italy, two Ryanair flights were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following potential bomb threats, according to the airport operator ADR. The first was a flight from Lisbon, while a second later in the morning from Dublin was escorted in by Italian air force fighter jets until landing.

Bulgaria’s ​transport ‌ministry said ‌in a statement to ‌Reuters that threats were ​made against a Wizz Air flight ⁠from Bergamo and a Ryanair flight from Dublin to ⁠the capital, Sofia. Both flights were carrying about 180 passengers and landed safely, with no devices found.
The separate incidents came the day after a Wizz Air service from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet.
The plane, which was due to depart from Luton at 8.15am on Monday for Sofia, was diverted after a bomb threat was received “during the flight”, Wizz Air said.
Airlines abide by a regulated process to assess and manage bomb threats, although virtually all are fake. In the UK, airlines file a mandatory occurrence report to the Civil Aviation Authority.
Ryanair did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: US strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
articles.summary: Strikes on eve of US midterms reportedly target surface-to-air missiles being used against US assets
body: The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, hours after the vice-president, JD Vance, said he was optimistic that diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

The strikes, disclosed by Iranians on social media and confirmed by US Central Command (Centcom), came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters. Diplomatic mediators believe it will be clear within two days whether the basis for continued indirect talks between the US and Iran exists.

The US tried to downplay the significance of the attacks by stressing they were limited and not the precursor of a much-anticipated major assault on Iran that Trump has promised after the midterms if the US adjudges Iran’s nuclear program continues as a threat to the west.
The US described the strikes as defensive in nature, aimed at missile batteries from which Iranian attacks on US planes had been mounted the day before.

Inside Iran, blame was initially placed on Israel, but later it was conceded that the US was responsible. Israel itself insisted it had no role in the attacks. Similar military exchanges have happened at least three times since the cessation of major hostilities, as the US and Iran jostle for control of the strait.

Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, referring to the overnight US strikes, said: “We are still in a state of war. The aggression against Iran has not ended in our view, and until the military aggression is completely and permanently terminated Iran has the right to legitimate defence.”
He added Iran was not waiting for the results from the midterms to adjust its negotiating position, saying: “We do not tie our foreign policies to the elections of other countries.”

Iran would like to see Trump weakened in those elections, but recognises the two-month interlude between the elections and the start of the newly elected Congress represents the point of maximum tension.

Chief negotiator Mohammad Ghalibaf made no direct mention of the attacks during an address to parliament, but said any miscalculation by the US would lead to an unpredictable Iranian response. In common with other Iranian leaders, he suggested the attacks would extend to US bases in Europe. Maps of Nato bases in Europe have appeared on the front page of the more conservative newspapers, implying they will be targets in any war.

The greater concern in Tehran appears to be the apparent inability of Qatari mediators to bridge the gap between Iran and the US over the upfront commitments Iran must make to end its nuclear program irreversibly, a phrase used by JD Vance.

It was Vance, in a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the supreme national security council, who proposed the restart of talks, but so far those talks have not led to any direct contact between the US and Iranian sides.

On Tuesday Rezaei appeared to reject the US response as inadequate, saying on X: “America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.” The seven conditions include the unfreezing of Iran assets abroad, and the lifting of sanctions on oil exports.

Iran has offered to lift the blockade on the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US lifting economic constraints on Iran. Once those two days, elapse Iran would also enter into talks about its nuclear program, but Tehran has refused to give upfront concessions either about the return of UN inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites or to agree to ship the 400kg of highly enriched uranium to a third country. The most likely compromise is a down-blending of the stockpile inside Iran under international supervision, and with an external guarantor, such as China.

Esmail Baghaei, the foreign ministry spokesman, struck a pessimistic note saying the US attitude to Iran’s nuclear program was “the biggest and most costly lie of the century”, and was fundamentally based on having a problem with Iran as an idea and historical entity.
Related: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war

Qatar said its mediation was continuing, and there was a very high level of coordination by countries in the region. Most of these Gulf states know they will be attacked by Iran if the US mounts an assault, and are desperate to avoid further damage to their fraying economies. Majed al-Ansari, the spokesman for the Qatar foreign ministry, insisted both sides remained committed to the process.
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effect on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

However, he said the US might still “have to go after Pickaxe Mountain” – referring to a fortified underground site in central Iran that is suspected to be a nuclear facility – but said it would not be a “big deal” and could be done in “one hour”.

Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices, as his administration touted renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections.

articles.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
articles.summary: Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region
body: China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.

The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.

Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”

Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.

Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”

As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.

Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.

The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.

Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.

Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

articles.title: Russia bombs humanitarian hub in Ukraine, killing at least 31 people
articles.summary: Other overnight strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people
body: Russia has bombed a humanitarian hub in southern Ukraine, killing at least 31 people and leaving dozens missing, as part of a wave of strikes across the country.

Other overnight Russian strikes targeted power plants across Ukraine, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people, as the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned that the US was distracted by its midterm elections.
In total, Russia had launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, Zelenskyy said in an online post.

“The Russians think America won’t notice this signal of theirs,” he said. “But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes,” he said.
The barrage came just a day after a rare local ceasefire in neighbouring Kherson ended, underscoring the limits of the temporary truce.

The deadliest guided-bomb attack first targeted a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region, and then took aim at a nearby shelter.

The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the regional military administration, said on Tuesday. At least five people were hurt. Semikin said 48 people were considered missing.
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials.
Related: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app

Efforts to rescue people on Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.

The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky, brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” Zelenskyy said.

In the north-east region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack had wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said. A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients had been transferred to other medical facilities, said the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Syniehubov.

“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people,” Zelenskyy said.

The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky. It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine were due to resume next week, the US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
Donald Trump, who pledged during his election campaign to end the war in a single day, has repeatedly pushed for a settlement but has so far failed to secure a breakthrough.

The latest round of talks is scheduled for 10-11 November in Abu Dhabi, according to Witkoff, amid growing concerns in Kyiv and among its European allies over Trump’s increasingly close ties with Moscow and discussions of potential business deals between the US and Russia.
Russia announced on Tuesday that its delegation would be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline former culture minister who has headed several previous rounds of negotiations with Ukraine.

Medinsky’s earlier appointment as chief negotiator was met with scepticism by Ukrainian officials and analysts, who questioned whether he had the authority to make meaningful concessions. A key architect of the historical revisionism used by Putin to justify his invasion of Ukraine, Medinsky has long promoted the Kremlin’s narrative that Ukraine is inseparable from Russia.

Zelenskyy, meanwhile, arrived in Berlin for talks with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Germany has become Ukraine’s largest provider of military aid since Merz took office in May 2025, overtaking the US as American support has declined.
The Ukrainian president is also expected to attend this year’s Berlin Security Conference.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Are prediction markets accurate on elections? The US midterms are a big test
articles.summary: Polymarket and Kalshi have risen for collecting the ‘wisdom of crowds’. But after high-profile blunders, some wonder if their predictions were just ‘stupid people getting lucky’
body: Just as voting was due to end in Brazil’s presidential runoff on 25 October, a supreme court justice ordered polling stations to stay open for another two hours, to give voters stranded by flash floods and bus shortages more time to cast their ballots. It added more drama to an already tense election. The final polls the night before showed Flávio Bolsonaro only marginally ahead, by about 51% to 49% – within the margin of error. A statistical tie.

Prediction markets told a different story. Polymarket priced a Bolsonaro victory at about 80% on election day, where it had hovered for three weeks. On the eve of the vote it touched 84%. Even as polls closed, the market gave the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, roughly a one-in-five chance. A few hours later, Lula had won, by 51.8% to 48.2%.

Prediction markets claim to be highly accurate because they aggregate the independent judgments of many traders – the “wisdom of crowds” – and make each one put money behind their beliefs. Prices are more accurate than polls and faster than newsrooms, proponents argue. So what went wrong?
Related: On Polymarket, ‘privileged’ users made millions betting on war strikes and diplomatic strategy. What did they know beforehand?

As Americans prepare to vote in the first midterms since prediction markets broke into the mainstream, the question has taken on new significance. The founders of Polymarket and Kalshi evangelise market efficiency as a kind of secular faith. They promise a more accurate way to forecast the future, one that harnesses the collective intelligence of traders with money on the line.

But Brazil was not a one-off. Across a string of high-profile elections, the markets have been confidently wrong. Meanwhile, the more money flows into election contracts, the more there is to gain from distorting them or exploiting privileged information. The US midterms – the night prediction markets have been waiting for – will be their biggest test to date and potentially a referendum on their authority.

In recent weeks, traders have swarmed to wager on Brazil’s neck-and-neck presidential race, Israel’s election deadlock and the open question of who will control the US Congress. In October 2022, before the last midterms, trading volume on Polymarket and Kalshi combined reached just over $4m, according to data from DefiLlama. Over the same period before the 2024 presidential election, it surpassed $90m. This October: $21bn. A monthly record.

Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell binary contracts on real-world events: will this thing happen, yes or no? As contracts change hands, their prices fluctuate, producing a continuously updating estimate of the probability of an outcome.

A few years ago, prediction markets were basically fringe betting sites. But under Donald Trump – whose pick for CFTC chair, Mike Selig, a former lawyer for Polymarket and Kalshi, has fought to bring and keep the industry onshore – prediction markets have emerged from the fringes of finance. Event contracts “help the public forecast, plan for, hedge, and even harness” perceptions of future outcomes, and can “sometimes forecast outcomes better than polling”, the CFTC states on its website.

Out of exile, the platforms have enmeshed themselves in public life. Newsrooms including the AP, CNN, the Wall Street Journal and CNBC have signed deals to integrate live election odds into their coverage. In a recent interview about the midterms, the former congressman Brad Carson cited one candidate’s “99% chance to win on Polymarket”. He made no reference to polls.

Polymarket is “the most accurate thing we have as mankind right now, until someone else creates some sort of a super crystal ball”, its founder and chief executive, Shayne Coplan, told 60 Minutes last year.

Prediction markets have a record of getting things right. An analysis of Polymarket transactions over two years found that markets priced at about 80% resolved “yes” roughly 80% of the time. Across the full range of prices, outcomes rarely strayed more than a few percentage points from the probabilities the prices implied.
But in several recent high-profile elections, markets have gotten things wrong.

The same day as Brazil’s runoff, Serbia held a snap parliamentary election. The day before, Polymarket gave Aleksandar Vučić’s United Serbia a 70% chance of winning. On election night, the opposition Student List, born out of nearly two years of anti-corruption protests, took 52.6% of the vote. Vučić conceded, securing just 39.2%.

In August, Polymarket and Kalshi gave Francesca Hong roughly a 95% chance in the Wisconsin Democratic governor’s primary. Her rival, David Crowley, won by less than half a percentage point. Polymarket then deleted an X post saying Hong had a 96% chance.
On the eve of the Los Angeles mayoral primary in June, both platforms gave the reality TV star Spencer Pratt about a 75% chance of advancing to the runoff. He finished third.

In March, on the morning of Illinois’s Democratic Senate primary, Kalshi priced Raja Krishnamoorthi – who had spent nearly $30m on the race – at 61%. His opponent, Juliana Stratton won, despite the crypto industry, which is closely tied to prediction markets, spending nearly $10m opposing her campaign.
The day before New York City’s 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, Polymarket gave Andrew Cuomo a 66% chance of winning. Zohran Mamdani beat him by 12 points.
Why did a “super crystal ball” diverge so drastically from polls on these occasions?

Firstly, it’s important to consider that prices and election polls measure different things. The former captures the odds that a candidate will win on election day, whereas polling margins reflect a candidate’s lead. For that reason, Polymarket percentages often accentuate small polling gaps. For instance, latest polling data from FiftyPlusOne shows a 2% margin between Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn in Nebraska’s Senate race, but Kalshi and Polymarket have a Ricketts win at about 70% as of Monday afternoon. In Ohio’s governor race, polls show Vivek Ramaswamy within a few points of Amy Acton, whereas Kalshi and Polymarket have an Acton win at 82% as of Monday afternoon.
So, in cases like Brazil’s election, Polymarket’s 80% forecast of Bolsonaro victory looked wildly inaccurate compared with a two-point polling margin.

Prediction markets became popular in 2024 precisely because they saw what pollsters couldn’t. Polymarket and Kalshi predicted Trump’s victory weeks before results emerged, all while polls projected a toss-up. But researchers note the US presidential election wasn’t necessarily proof of the crowd’s wisdom.

To assess whether prices accurately and efficiently aggregate political information, researchers at Vanderbilt University analysed 2,500 political prediction markets during the final five weeks of the presidential race involving more than $2.3bn in transactions. The study found markets “often behaved in ways inconsistent with rational information aggregation”. Accuracy fell to 67% and 78% on Polymarket and Kalshi respectively, while prices “diverged sharply across markets, exchanges, and contract types”.

Deciphering why markets get things wrong in some elections, and right in others, can be challenging. Pollsters can scrutinise their sampling methods; on prediction markets, traders are anonymous and their reasoning largely opaque. Experts say it comes down to the breakdown of market volume between retail traders – casual, recreational users who use a vibes-based approach to betting – versus a skilled minority of full-time traders who build statistical models incorporating vast datasets. Growing research suggests that accuracy across the board owes less to the wisdom of the crowd than to a small minority of skilled traders.

The idea of the “wisdom of crowds” is commonly traced to the statistician Francis Galton, who in 1907 observed that the average of hundreds of guesses about the weight of an ox at a country fair came remarkably close to its actual weight. Aggregating many independent judgments, the principle goes, can beat individual experts.

But prediction markets don’t really work like that. A recent study found that just 1% of Polymarket accounts captured three-quarters of profits since 2022, with the top 0.1% taking half. Two-thirds of accounts have lost money. At the top are the so-called “sharps”: skilled traders who hunt for mispriced odds, exploiting advantages in knowledge, data and speed – and potentially insiders. At the bottom are recreational bettors, known to sharps as “dumb money” or “fish”, who often trade on instinct.
One Polymarket trader, a mathematics PhD known as “@gopfan”, has made nearly $2m over the past two years using statistical models to forecast elections around the world.

It is less the wisdom of crowds than “the wisdom of the informed”, as Theis Ingerslev Jensen, an assistant professor of finance at Yale University, puts it. A study he co-authored this year estimates that just 3% of Polymarket accounts belong to skilled traders, whose activity drives prices towards more accurate probabilities.

That model works in a quiet market, with a few well-informed gamblers. It breaks down in a loud one. When a high-profile election arrives, a wave of recreational money floods in – often from people treating a bet as a show of support rather than a prediction. The data-driven sharps can push back, but only with the capital they have. Once that is committed, nobody is left to correct the price.

High-profile elections attract “extremely, extremely high” volumes of recreational trading, says @gopfan, making the odds “sometimes pretty ridiculous”. Brazil was a case in point: “The prices were staying extremely distorted because all the sharp money was already allocated into the market. There was no one to move it back.”
Related: Gambling addicts are struggling as Kalshi and Polymarket explode in the US: ‘You could be betting your rent away’

Brazil’s crowd also had reasons to be confidently wrong. Bolsonaro won the first round by 47% to 45%, and since the two-round system began in 1989, no candidate had overcome a first-round defeat to win the runoff. His odds surged, suggesting traders may have treated a precedent drawn from a handful of elections as an iron rule. They may also have underestimated the significance of 33 million first-round abstainers, who leaned towards Lula. And Brazil’s April ban on prediction markets may have left the market dominated by foreigners, less attuned to local politics – though bans can be circumvented with VPNs, as Polymarket users in the US did until a year ago.

Why, then, did the markets correctly favour Trump in 2024, when a flood of new traders appeared to treat their bets as proxy votes? “Sometimes stupid people just get lucky,” says @gopfan. “They win just because they are randomly right. But it’s nothing more than a pure coincidence.”
“They were lucky to some extent, right?” Jensen agrees.

The flood also explains which way the markets lean. One trader who profited from the 2024 influx, @yungstalin, has made nearly $1m on Polymarket. Shortly after joining, he noticed a “very clear pattern” among new accounts: they were Trump supporters. “The vast majority of recreational bettors were just dumping money on Trump, and making the most basic mistakes,” he says. His strategy was simple: “Just follow the dumb people and bet against them.”

In 2024, the dumb money happened to back the winner. In Brazil, Serbia and Los Angeles, it did not. When it comes to using Polymarket to judge the midterms results, the wisdom of the crowds really depends on the wisdom of the individuals.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Britain is moving the goalposts for its migrant workers
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Shabana Mahmood has softened rules for care workers after an outcry, but thousands of other migrant workers face an uncertain future
body: Good morning. “Settlement should not be automatic, it should be earned,” home secretary Shabana Mahmood told the Commons yesterday as she unveiled a radical shake-up of the rules governing how long foreign workers and refugees have to wait before they are granted the right to live in the UK indefinitely.

What Mahmood insisted was a “fair solution” that would cut welfare spending by billions had been characterised as the first serious test of whether Andy Burnham could keep the left of the Labour party in line, after the original plans were met with outrage from backbenchers, migrants rights groups and unions.

In the event she avoided outright revolt, but was accused of watering down more punitive proposals to appease her party critics, while charities are furious at stringent new requirements for refugees, and legal experts warned retrospective rule changes now faced by many migrant workers undermine the rule of law.

In an endeavour to sift the substance from the spin, I spoke to home affairs editor, Rajeev Syal, about the detail of the plans and community affairs correspondent, Chris Osuh, about the people whose lives they will change.

Commonwealth summit | Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.

Defence | British troops and their European allies would be allowed to fire back if attacked by Russians when potentially stationed as peacekeepers in Ukraine after a ceasefire, western officials said.

Iran | The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

Sweden | Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C, echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

US midterms | Donald Trump unveiled the delayed results of his $14m renovation of Washington DC’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool in what is expected to be his final press conference before voters head to the polls for the midterm elections.

The home secretary wanted to double the wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR), to 10 years for new arrivals, as well as retrospectively for those who came in the post-Brexit wave. Some lower-paid migrants, including care workers, would have to wait 15 years.
The proposals caused controversy. Unions described the plans for retrospective changes for much-needed care workers as “cruel and unconscionable”.

A year later the political context is very different. Andy Burnham has succeeded Starmer, and the threat posed to Labour by Reform has receded significantly, while net migration is plummeting. But migration remains a top concern for voters, and YouGov polling released yesterday found that nearly half of Britons support extending the waiting period for legal migrants before they are granted ILR.

Meantime, the criticism of Mahmood’s plans has only become more vocal. In June, while still on the backbenches before her promotion back to cabinet, Angela Rayner said the care worker proposal was “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.
And last weekend, the Guardian reported on a letter signed by parliamentarians alongside campaigners and health professionals describing the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

Ahead of the statement, there were reports of up to 100 Labour MPs ready to rebel if Mahmood didn’t soften her original proposals – though quite how is unclear, because she doesn’t require a vote on primary legislation to put through these changes.

In the event, no rebellion was necessary. While Mahmood has tightened the rules on ILR significantly, doubling the standard wait to qualify to 10 years, she scrapped her planned 15 year wait for lower-paid workers.

As Rajeev sets out in this helpful explainer, under pressure from health unions, the home secretary offered a carve-out for care workers, allowing an estimated 280,000 and their dependents to apply for ILR after five years.

Faster routes will be available for highest band taxpayers, for example, and some public service workers including doctors, nurses and teachers. But, as Rajeev points out, thousands of lower-paid workers will still face the shock of having to wait a decade before being able to apply to settle in the UK, despite being told when they first arrived the wait was five years. The changes will mean half a million people face longer waits for settled status.

“The new rules also place particularly stringent requirements for settlement on refugees,” Rajeev tells me – with those entering via small boat set to wait up to 30 years for permanent settlement and those claiming asylum having entered the country legally waiting a decade. The Refugee Council condemned the plans as “unfair and unworkable” and likely to harm refugee integration. The Law Society went further, suggesting the new rules contravene the Refugee Convention.
The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes like the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.

Both Zack Polanski and Kemi Badenoch, politicians at either end of the political spectrum, have dismissed care work as “wiping bottoms” in recent years. There’s a crude assumption that, because it is poorly paid, it must demand minimal effort. But I know from my own family’s experience of social care about the patience, skill and humanity involved in this kind of work.

It was the prospect of even more overwhelming uncertainty that people found so crushing, Chris Osuh tells me. He has been interviewing care workers around Manchester about their professional conditions since the changes were first mooted: “When somebody’s waiting for settlement, the uncertainty never goes away”. And the practical reality is that during this waiting period individuals are still paying out visa costs on top of taxes, while their career ambitions and earning capacity may be limited because some jobs are contingent on having secured ILR. “Basically it makes your life a lot more precarious for longer.”

It’s worth reiterating that these changes affect people who’ve arrived legally in the UK through pathways intended to help British people. “You’re doing vital, hard, underpaid work where there are huge skill shortages”, he says. It’s also the case that some care workers find themselves tied to exploitative employers by strict visa arrangements, something Mahmood acknowledged yesterday when she introduced safety nets for those exploited by “rogue sponsors”.

Data suggests 19% of the care workforce are non-EU citizens, and many come from places such as Nigeria, Ghana and broader sub-Saharan Africa. As the prime minister opens dialogue around apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, it’s hard not to see this as “a continuation of an exploitative relationship”, adds Chris. “Once again, Britain looks to all those countries that it once colonised to replace the labour that was lost during Brexit”.

Even before Mahmood stood up to make her statement, Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, was accusing her of surrendering to “the open-borders Labour left” while Nigel Farage, whose Reform UK party wants to get rid of ILR completely, claimed she was “losing the fight with the far left”.

Unions representing care workers welcomed the concessions yesterday evening, while care sector bosses expressed relief that they weren’t about to lose a whole tranche of their workforce. But Rajeev cautions against reading these compromises purely as capitulation to Unison, one of Labour’s biggest financial backers, or to avoid cabinet rancour.

“If you look at the plans as a whole,” he tells me, “aside from the compromise around care workers, this still amounts to a radical hardening of policy that she has pushed through. And Andy Burnham supports it because he wants to win back the ‘red wall’.”

“This is about fairness in a system that Burnham’s already expressed a very personal interest in,” says Rajeev. Burnham has repeatedly praised the dedication of care home staff who looked after his father, Roy, before his death in September. But Burnham has also reiterated that his version of fairness is one that passes the Makerfield test.

As our political editor Pippa Crerar puts it in this analysis, the prime minister regards migration as a means to show people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government is prepared to listen and act. The next challenge for Mahmood is to convince the public of exactly that.
